name: Claimatic Optimization Problem
body: Claimatic Optimization Problem  We Have a 70 gig table on AWS in MySQL called the claims table. It is regular MySQL, not Aurora. It has a million records. It’s only 70 gigs because it has a long text field called assignment notes. Otherwise it would only have been a 1 gig table We have the data for the assignment notes field stored in another table Querying the claims table takes a long time because of this field Our 3rd party dev team said you can’t just drop the assignment notes column from the table. Because it’s innodb, you would not gain back performance, by doing that. You would have to drop and re-create Our plan is to make a new table with all the same fields and all the same data, except for assignment notes since we have that duplicated somewhere else Once that’s done, we could finally drop the 70 gig table, and rename the new table to the claims table name I was thinking to write the script to accomplish this in Python We could make a jobs table to keep track of its progress since we could only run this table at night  What is the best way to do this?

name: I’m on a dev team. We have a PLC SAAS website. PLC means professional…
body: I’m on a dev team. We have a PLC SAAS website. PLC means professional learning coaching, which in our case is public schools. Our website allows you to create  coaching session, add attendees, check off performance indicators, make plans for th teacher to improve. We already have an AI module that allows coaches to get feedback on custom content based on knowledge bases that are custom per district. We are using Amazon Bedrock. All of our stack is on AWS. Our site is in Yii PHP with MySQL and we also have a separate API site in Python fast API. We want to implement RAG and allow Amazon Bedrock to access some of our PHP API endpoints. It could then read coaching log information or even create coaching logs. We have decided we want to build an MPC server for this. We have an authentication plan. We will create an API key field per user record that the user would have to paste into the prompt for whatever app accesses our MCP server. Once we got the user record tied to it, we would request a bearer token, and send that back to the app, which would then authenticate to our MCP server with that bearer token. So we’re building an MCP server. We think it might be best to use built in libraries for this. I think we should do it in Python but I am also open to golang. body: Engage RTC for our RTEs Looked into what new advancements have happened for RTE collaborations so that we can fix our codox problems .   There have been a lot of really good advancements that we could definitely benefit from, such as collaboration engines that handle merge conflicts with live updates way better such as Yj’s.   Some of the benefits of doing this correctly, is something called ephemeral awareness, where we can actually see who else is in this document and have different colors for their cursors like in Google Docs. That’s just something that comes along with these libraries.  There are a few components in this process of setting up RTC the proper way   RTE - angular (would have to change from TinyMCE - one called Lexical uses toolbar that looks a lot like Google Docs) Collaboration Engine - Angular Collaboration Backend (web socket)  - Self hosted NodeJS server or 3rd party paid service (expensive) MySQL database (we have)  Redis (optional but needed in order to scale)  From my research, I would say, unless we’re willing to spend a lot of money every month to pay for a 3rd party service to be the collaboration backend (1 to 2k per month possibly), this is quite a big project. Self-hosting it in AWS in a way that can scale, and setting this up in all environments, makes it a heavy project. (For production, multiple node JS instances behind a Load balancer, redis)

name: Ideas for FastAPI Presentation
body: Ideas for FastAPI Presentation FastAPI functions a lot like Yii, they follow a lot of the same patterns that any MVC framework would use You have a route, that route is connected to a specific controller and method on that controller  That controller authenticates and takes in the request, does any permission checks that need to be done And then it queries the database with some type of ORM And then it returns a JSON response  Compare a Yii controller with a FastAPI route  The main thing we will be adjusting to is using FastAPIs ORM, which in this case is SQLAlchemy How do write data models and migrations, and how do we query and save data  Compare a Yii Data model with a Fast API Data Model  So with a functioning framework, all we really need to do is manage routes which take in the request, query with ORM, or update the data with ORM, and then return a response, usually with a resultset NOTE: A lot of times instead of directly querying the ORM, in Fast API we would make a service that does what we would have done with an ORM query and then just call that service and return data. Might be a bit overkill but that’s common practice in FastAPI  Pydantic models  are kind of like DTOS Their just object field definitions You define the request post body as well as the return resultset body Which is great for 2 things First, it validates the request, and if you send something that doesn’t match the request definition it tells you what you did wrong. Also defines the response  Swagger is generated automatically at this route   http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs  It also uses all the request and response definitions and other things in the route So that it can add all that stuff to swagger  So that it shows you exactly how the request should be sent, and doesn’t allow you to send it any other way. Collections in Postman - also, if you still prefer to use Postman, you can easily import the open api spec into postman as a collection, and there’s no limits to how many times you do that as long as you import it as a collection  http://localhost:8000/openapi.json  Postman > Import button at top left Select paste, upload or URL  can’t use docker URL cuz it’s not publicly accessible Be sure to select Collection. You get unlimited collections, but you only get like 3 API builders one  Inside routes Inside the routes it’s basically just ORM it does abstract the calling of the ORM into CRUD services which are just modular functions for each model that do things like get a data object by id or get all data objects Those are located in /services/crud How ORM works DB Models - which are the equivalent of Yii ORM Data Models Compare Yii and FastAPI side by side  Like Yii Defines fields Contains relationships Different from Yii I don’t know if you can create model functions Mostly just fields and relationships Also does migrations, but I’d rather not show that yet. There’s some kinks I want to work out with how we use it

body: Reasons Why Airbyte Issue can’t be fixed Problem I fixed in Custom ETL The main problem I was encountering is with the query that parses JSON and joins to the view that selects the submission data When you parse a json field, the field in the query becomes a super object, that can have properties on it containing arrays of items or other fields. In the submission data json, the fieldId GUID which is how we identify a question on a form, is came-case. The problem is that redshift 1.0.1 treats these all as lowercase and so can’t allow you to access a field on a super object that has uppercase letters In my code, I have string replaced field id to be all lowercase and so it fixed the problem  Dealing with same issue in airbyte I don’t think we can do the same thing in airbyte. Even if I change it, the sync will just change it back. name: ETL - Problems that I’m fixing, what I’ve found
body: ETL - Problems that I’m fixing, what I’ve found  Problems I’m Fixing Can’t rebuild from scratch efficiently Don’t want to have to use a sync table in MySQL   Other problems I need to solve Improve efficiency of existing update and insert incremental updates  Use delete proceed the same way as before Use merge into to do this since our version of redshift supports it Have a better way to not let the keys degrade Correctly do the loading tables full replace, and still not let the keys degrade Preserve computing power by not always doing a full replace  Handle a complete re-indexing whenever we want   Notes to remember  We still need to detect if the table is empty and do a full replace regardless of the size of the data We have to support full replace for all loading tables We need a CSV folder for the simple dim tables, in the python elt repo What this means is we should be able to completely rebuild all loading tables, and all public tables are already rebuilt. No part of the script should rely on anything from airbyte Use that same type of thinking to bootstrap the deploy to production  Eventually wipe out loading_target on staging and rebuild from scratch You can have create tables statements for the new loading target be like running a dump. They can be a sql file on the python elt repo First, e2l Etl sets itself up on itself into loading target Then staging sets up a new loading target on itself into own Then we do the same thing in production Working on all this will iron out most of deployment plan  Solutions We can use python pandas to create CSVs from MySQL and use COPY to put them into redshift as a full replace We can run check to see if we should run and then run VACCUM and ANALYZE every time we sync  Also, we should ANALYZE and VACCUM the same way for he public tables truncate and insert For the other tables that use incremental syncs, we can do the updates and inserts as a MERGE INTO which is much faster than other methods Delete process will work the same as before  For this we don’t need to use VACUUM and ANALYZE as often ￼ Using these two strategies, we no longer need to rebuild sort and distribution keys with a ctas statement We are still using staging tables

Add chopped onion and minced garlic to the pot, and cook until the onion is translucent, about 3-4 minutes. Pour in the chicken broth and diced tomatoes, and bring to a simmer.
